query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges when grain-boundary segregation and subsequent nanoscale precipitate formation reach a critical threshold under service-like thermal exposures, thereby reducing grain-boundary cohesion and shifting the fracture mode from ductile to brittle despite the overall stabilized single-phase matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a nearly homogeneous grain-boundary chemistry.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal aging treatments that simulate service conditions known to promote grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitation without inducing significant grain coarsening.
generation.conditions: The alloy is tested under service-relevant high-temperature exposures followed by standard mechanical loading (e.g., fracture toughness or bending tests) at ambient or sub-ambient temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional changes at grain boundaries leading to the nucleation of nanoscale intergranular precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Thermally induced grain-boundary segregation fosters the formation of brittle intermetallic precipitates at the grain boundaries. These precipitates reduce the intergranular cohesion, thereby promoting a brittle fracture mode despite the inherent toughness of the matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogenously processed alloy, thermally aged samples will exhibit reduced toughness and a shift from ductile (transgranular) to brittle (intergranular) fracture modes. Mechanical tests are expected to show lower ductility and fracture resistance in the aged samples.
generation.baseline: The as-processed high-entropy alloy with minimal grain-boundary segregation and an absence of significant intergranular precipitates, displaying high ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under service conditions where the thermal exposure is sufficient to induce grain-boundary segregative effects without causing overall grain coarsening or deleterious intermetallic growth throughout the bulk material.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold levels of grain-boundary segregant concentration and precipitate volume fraction that lead to embrittlement are uncertain and may vary with the specific alloy composition and environmental loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical samples of the single-phase high-entropy alloy. Subject subsets to a range of controlled thermal aging treatments designed to incrementally increase grain-boundary segregation without inducing extensive grain coarsening. Conduct mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness and bending tests) on each subset alongside detailed microstructural characterization (using techniques such as APT or EDS mapping) to quantify grain-boundary compositional changes and precipitate formation.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of grain-boundary segregant concentration and precipitate volume fraction
Fracture mode characterization (ductile vs brittle) from mechanical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to increased thermal aging (and hence elevated grain-boundary segregation) do not display a statistically significant decrease in toughness or a shift towards intergranular (brittle) fracture relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitate formation mediate brittle behavior in these alloys will be falsified.

citation_validation.initial_error: generated hypothesis cites unavailable evidence: ['Gludovatz et al. (2014)', 'Studies on grain-boundary segregation in complex concentrated alloys']

recalled_precedents.study: Gludovatz et al. (2014) on High-Entropy Alloys
recalled_precedents.approach: Investigated the strength–ductility trade-off in HEAs using detailed mechanical testing combined with microstructural characterization (via TEM and APT) to correlate local compositional fluctuations and phase stability with mechanical performance.
recalled_precedents.finding: Demonstrated that while overall compositional complexity stabilizes the matrix, localized compositional deviations at grain boundaries can lead to nanoscale ordering or precipitation that influences ductility and toughness.

recalled_precedents.study: Various studies on grain-boundary segregation in complex concentrated alloys
recalled_precedents.approach: Employed controlled thermal treatments and minor alloying additions to manipulate grain-boundary composition, with subsequent mechanical testing and atom-probe tomography to quantify segregation effects.
recalled_precedents.finding: Found that even in cases of high overall compositional complexity, increased grain-boundary segregation correlates with reduced intergranular cohesion and a shift toward brittle failure modes.
